Echidna. In Greek mythology, Echidna is a monstrous creature, part woman and part serpent, who serves as the progenitor of numerous classical monsters. Paired with the Titan Typhon, Echidna bore the most fearsome beasts of Greek myth, making her the symbolic source of chaos and danger in the mythological cosmos.

Echidna is depicted as a woman from the waist up with a serpent's tail below, though some sources describe her as more fully serpentine with only human features. Her mother was Medusa, the Gorgon slain by Perseus, a genealogy that connects Echidna to ancient serpent deities and chthonic, or underworld, powers. Her union with Typhon, a primordial storm giant, produced the most famous monsters of Greek mythology. Cerberus, the three-headed hound guarding the underworld, came from this union, as did the Hydra of Lerna, a nine-headed serpent slain by Heracles, and the Chimera, a composite monster with lion, goat, and serpent parts. Her offspring also included Orthus, a two-headed dog, and Ladon, the hundred-headed dragon guarding the golden apples of the Hesperides, and Pegasus, the divine horse, though some accounts vary on his parentage.

Echidna herself lived in a cave, sometimes said to be in the underworld or at the edge of the known world, representing the borderland between civilization and primal chaos. She is less frequently featured as a character in myths than her offspring. Her primary role is genealogical, explaining the origin of monsters and connecting them to each other and to older divine and chthonic powers. In Hesiod's Theogony, which provides the most detailed account of her, Echidna represents a bridge between the Titans and the monsters that would challenge the Olympian gods.
